title: A Wardrobe for the Postcards
premise: After his mother's funeral, Mirabel Halloran finds a shoebox of unsent postcards addressed to a woman named Odile, all written from the childhood house now scheduled for auction. Cataloging the house's contents for the estate sale, he discovers that his mother spent decades as Odile's ghostwriter — and that the celebrated memoirs published under Odile's name were stolen from his mother's drafts. As the auction approaches, Mirabel must decide whether to expose the truth and destroy the loyalty his mother kept until her death, or let the silence stand. In the end, he reads one postcard aloud at the auction, claims authorship on his mother's behalf, and forgives both women — keeping the wardrobe, not the house.
about_author: Sable Quintana is the pen name of a former estate appraiser who spent fifteen years cataloguing other people's belongings before writing about them. She lives near the coast, where she collects postcards she never sends.

chapters.title: The Tenant's Key
chapters.summary: Mirabel, POV. Three weeks after the funeral, he moves through his mother's flat cataloguing her possessions for probate, feeling like a renter in his own grief. He finds nothing personal — no letters, no photographs — and realizes she curated even him. Emotional beat: hollow disorientation.

chapters.title: A Shoebox of Weather
chapters.summary: Mirabel, POV. At the bottom of a wardrobe he finds forty-one unsent postcards, all addressed to an 'Odile Vasseur,' each describing weather in a town he doesn't recognize. The handwriting is unmistakably his mother's. Beat: first crack of curiosity piercing numbness.

chapters.title: The House Goes Under the Hammer
chapters.summary: Mirabel, POV. A solicitor's letter announces that the childhood house in that very town — left jointly to Mirabel and a stranger — will be auctioned in six weeks unless co-heirs agree otherwise. The stranger is Odile Vasseur. Beat: the past acquires an address and a deadline.

chapters.title: Arrival in Saltglass
chapters.summary: Mirabel, POV. He travels to Saltglass and stands outside the shuttered house, remembering summers he'd half-invented. A neighbor mistakes him for his mother and goes pale. Beat: uncanny return; the town remembers what he doesn't.

chapters.title: Odile at the Gate
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. Now seventy-eight and famous as the author of three acclaimed memoirs, Odile watches Mirabel from her window before finally meeting him at the gate, gracious and rehearsed. She offers tea and deflection in equal measure. Beat: charm as armor.

chapters.title: Inventory of Rooms
chapters.summary: Mirabel, POV. Hired by the auctioneers to inventory the house, he works room by room and finds his own childhood drawings filed under 'miscellaneous.' Someone lived here who knew him. Beat: tenderness tangled with suspicion.

chapters.title: The Memoirs on the Shelf
chapters.summary: Mirabel, POV. Reading Odile's celebrated first memoir in the house where it was supposedly written, he recognizes whole passages — rhythms, images — from the postcards' voice. Beat: cold recognition; the ground tilts.

chapters.title: What the Neighbor Saw
chapters.summary: Neighbor Ruth Ellery, POV. Ruth recalls two young women in this house in the sixties: one brilliant and invisible, one beautiful and ambitious. She never learned which was which, and chose not to ask. Beat: complicity of bystanders.

chapters.title: Confrontation Over Tea
chapters.summary: Mirabel and Odile, alternating. Mirabel lays the postcards on Odile's table. She neither denies nor confesses; instead she tells him how much his mother was loved, and how little she wanted credit. Beat: power shifting between guilt and control.

chapters.title: The Draft in the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Mirabel, POV. Inside the eponymous wardrobe, behind false backing, he finds a full manuscript draft titled in his mother's hand: 'The Salt Years.' It is the memoir, uncredited, dated two years before publication. Beat: proof arrives heavier than expected.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Argument
chapters.summary: Mirabel, POV. His mother's letters to a lawyer, also hidden, reveal she knew and chose silence — demanded it, even, as a condition of friendship. Mirabel rages at being made heir to someone else's bargain. Beat: anger at the dead.

chapters.title: The Auctioneer's Deadline
chapters.summary: Mirabel, POV. The auction house wants the wardrobe and its contents listed as sale lots within days. Legally, everything inside belongs to the estate — half of it Odile's. Time compresses. Beat: external pressure mounting.

chapters.title: Odile's Version
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. Odile narrates 1963: penniless, pregnant, and saved by Mirabel's mother, who traded her words for Odile's protection when the family threatened to have the child taken. Every theft had a ransom. Beat: sympathy destabilizes judgment.

chapters.title: Half an Heir
chapters.summary: Mirabel, POV. He learns Odile's son — raised as hers alone — was fathered by Mirabel's uncle, making the boy something like family. The silence protected more than reputations. Beat: the moral map grows complicated.

chapters.title: Reading the Salt Years
chapters.summary: Mirabel, POV. Through one long night he reads the manuscript and meets his mother's true voice for the first time — fierce, funny, unsentimental. Grief becomes acquaintance. Beat: love arriving too late but arriving.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. Odile proposes a settlement: she'll buy out Mirabel's share, fund the auction quietly, and take the manuscript to burn, leaving his mother's name buried as she wished. Generous, final, and a bribe. Beat: temptation dressed as mercy.

chapters.title: Ruth's Photograph
chapters.summary: Ruth, POV. Ruth gives Mirabel a photograph of the two young women laughing in the garden, arms linked — evidence of a friendship, not just a crime. He sees his mother happy and understands what silence cost her to keep. Beat: compassion complicating resolve.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Auction
chapters.summary: Mirabel, POV. Sleepless, he weighs exposure against obedience to the dead. He writes — then burns — a letter to his mother asking permission, realizing no answer is coming and the choice is his inheritance. Beat: decision crystallizing.

chapters.title: Lot Forty-One
chapters.summary: Mirabel, POV. At the auction, when the wardrobe comes up as Lot 41, Mirabel bids, wins it with nearly everything he has, and then, before the crowd, reads aloud the opening page of 'The Salt Years,' naming his mother as its author. Beat: climax — truth spoken publicly.

chapters.title: Odile Stands
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. In the stunned hall, Odile rises — not to deny but to confirm, telling the room whose sentences she borrowed and bowing her head. Public confession costs her reputation and buys her, at last, honesty. Beat: reckoning accepted.

chapters.title: Terms of Forgiveness
chapters.summary: Mirabel and Odile, alternating. Weeks later they meet: he declines her money but accepts her help publishing the manuscript under his mother's name. Forgiveness isn't absolution; it's a new arrangement. Beat: reconciliation without erasure.

chapters.title: The Postcard Finally Sent
chapters.summary: Mirabel, POV. On publication day, Mirabel mails the forty-first postcard — the only blank one — to Odile, now signed with his mother's name and a single line: 'Weather here is clear.' He keeps the wardrobe, empty, doors open. Beat: resolution — silence ended, memory owned.
